855.title: Subeg Singh and Shahbaz Singh
855.hook: a father and son executed in Lahore in 1745 for refusing to give up their faith
855.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Bhai Subeg Singh and Bhai Shahbaz Singh among the martyrs recalled in the daily Ardas, which remembers those who were broken on wheels rather than give up their faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mehtab Singh and Sukha Singh, two horses tied outside the gate at Amritsar. Your line was they rode in. What did you protect? Today, a quieter kind of courage, in Lahore. Day eight hundred fifty-five.

Some people live between two worlds. They work inside a system and belong to a community that system is hunting. They translate. They carry messages. They try to keep both sides talking. Subeg Singh was one of those people. Tradition says he was a Sikh who held a post with the government in Lahore, trusted enough to be sent with messages to the Khalsa. He had a son, Shahbaz Singh, a young man with his life ahead of him. Today: Subeg Singh and Shahbaz Singh.
screen: `BETWEEN TWO WORLDS.` → `A SIKH WITH A POST IN LAHORE.` → `A SON WITH HIS LIFE AHEAD.`

segments.voice: For a while, Subeg Singh's position kept his family safe. He was useful. He was a bridge. But the hunted years turned harder, and a bridge takes the strain from both sides. Tradition says the trouble began with the son. Shahbaz Singh was pressed to give up his faith, and he refused. Then the father was arrested too. Both were brought before the authorities in Lahore. And both, tradition says, were offered the same thing: their lives, if they would leave the Sikh path. What makes this story so hard to hear comes next. Tradition says the authorities did not only threaten them. They tried to use them against each other. A father can be broken through his son. A son can be broken through his father. Surely one of them would give way to save the other. Neither did. Tradition says they were put on the wheel, the charkhri, a torture that Sikhs name in the Ardas, the standing prayer, when they remember those who were broken on wheels and did not give up their faith. Tradition counts Subeg Singh and Shahbaz Singh among them, together. What the tradition dwells on is not only the pain. It's the strange kind of love in it. Either might have given his life for the other. What neither would do was ask the other to give up his faith. They held each other up by holding on. Father and son, side by side, each making the same refusal, and each, in a way, making it easier for the other.
screen: `A BRIDGE BETWEEN TWO WORLDS.` · `THE SON REFUSES. THE FATHER IS TAKEN.` · `USED AGAINST EACH OTHER.` · `NEITHER GIVES WAY.` · then, large: `FATHER AND SON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for fathers and sons, or simply hold them in mind. Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind a father and a son you know. Maybe your own father. Maybe your son. Maybe a pair you've watched from a distance, close or estranged. See them side by side. Notice what they carry for each other, and what lies between them. If you pray, you can hold them before Waheguru, saying the Name on each breath out. If you don't, just wish them well, breath by breath. The bell holds the time.
Subeg Singh. A father in Lahore, offered his life to give up his faith alongside his son Shahbaz Singh; neither would, and tradition counts them among the martyrs the Ardas recalls. Today's word.
Your line: father and son. Today, reach out to a father or a son in your life, with a call, a message, or a kind word about them. Day eight hundred fifty-five.

856.title: Captives freed from Nadir Shah
856.hook: in 1739 Sikh horsemen raided the retreating Persian army and freed captives
856.howItsDone: Sikhs retell the freeing of Nadir Shah's captives as part of the Khalsa's history of protecting the defenseless, and remember Guru Hargobind as Bandi Chhor, the freer of captives, at Bandi Chhor Divas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Subeg Singh and Shahbaz Singh, a father and son in Lahore who would not give way. Your line was father and son. Who did you reach out to? Day eight hundred fifty-six.

A long column moves along the road out of India. Camels and carts loaded with treasure. Soldiers. And among them, on foot, roped together, people who did not choose to be there: men and women taken from the cities the army had plundered, being marched toward a foreign country they would likely never leave. This was the army of Nadir Shah, the ruler of Persia, going home. Nobody, it seemed, could stop it. Then, at night, horsemen began to appear at the edges of the column. Today: captives freed from Nadir Shah.
screen: `A COLUMN OF TREASURE AND CAPTIVES.` → `NADIR SHAH GOES HOME.` → `HORSEMEN AT THE EDGES, AT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Nadir Shah had invaded from Persia and sacked Delhi. Tradition says his army left carrying not only treasure but captives. As it crossed the Punjab on the way back, it passed through the forests and river country where the Khalsa had been living on horseback. These were the riders this path met in the forests: hunted, scattered, with a price on their heads. They had every reason to stay out of the way of a conqueror's army. Instead, tradition says, the jathas struck the rear of the column again and again, in quick night raids. They took back some of the plunder. And they cut loose the captives. The Sikhs did not keep the freed people as prizes, or leave them by the road. Tradition says they escorted them back toward their homes and families. People who had been dragged away found themselves, a few days later, being walked home by strangers on horseback. Nadir Shah, it's said, asked the governor of Lahore who these raiders were. He was told they were Sikhs, that they had no homes but their saddles, and that they could not be caught. Nadir Shah is said to have replied that such people would one day rule the land. Whether he said it or not, Sikhs remember the exchange. The deeper thread is older than Nadir Shah. Sikhs call Guru Hargobind Bandi Chhor, the one who freed captives. In these years his Sikhs did the same, on horseback, at night.
screen: `AN ARMY GOING HOME WITH CAPTIVES.` · `NIGHT RAIDS ON THE REAR.` · `THE FREED ARE WALKED HOME.` · `NO HOMES BUT THEIR SADDLES.` · then, large: `CAPTIVES BROUGHT HOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: help someone get home. Settle, and breathe slowly. Bring to mind someone who is far from home right now, in any sense. A student a long way from family. A neighbor new to the country. Someone stuck in a hospital, a job or a situation they can't easily leave. A friend who has lost their way back to themselves. Picture one small thing that would bring them a step closer. A ride. A meal that tastes like home. A phone call. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Bandi Chhor, freer of captives. The name Sikhs give Guru Hargobind, echoed when his Sikhs cut loose the prisoners of a retreating Persian army and, tradition says, walked them home. Today's word.
Your line: captives brought home. Today, do one concrete thing to help someone get home, or feel a little closer to it. Day eight hundred fifty-six.

857.title: Why 1746 happened
857.hook: a governor's minister, grieving his brother, turned on the Sikhs, and the loss that followed is remembered as the small holocaust
857.howItsDone: Sikhs remember those who died in the eighteenth-century persecutions in the Ardas, the prayer said at the close of gurdwara gatherings, which honors the martyrs without cursing anyone.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sikh riders struck a departing army and the captives went back to their villages. Your line was captives brought home. Did you help anyone find their way back, even a little? Today, a darker turn. Day eight hundred fifty-seven.

A body is carried into Lahore. The dead man is Jaspat Rai, an official who rode out against a Sikh band and was killed in the fighting. His brother is Lakhpat Rai, a minister at the governor's court. Tradition says that when Lakhpat Rai heard, he took off his turban, threw it down, and swore he would not put it on again until he had wiped the Sikhs out. One man's grief. Soon it had an army behind it. This path has already walked through what happened next, the small holocaust. Today asks a different question. Not what happened, but why. Today: why 1746 happened.
screen: `A BROTHER KILLED.` → `A TURBAN THROWN DOWN.` → `A VOW OF REVENGE.`

segments.voice: Start with the grief, because it was real. Lakhpat Rai lost his brother. Nobody tells this story pretending that didn't hurt. But watch what the grief turned into. Tradition says he didn't stop at the fighters who had been in that clash. Sikhs living quietly in Lahore were rounded up. Tradition says he went further still: he ordered that the Sikh scriptures not be read, and even that the word gur, which means the Guru but is also the Punjabi word for brown sugar, not be spoken in the city. People were told to call the sugar something else. A man's sorrow had grown into a war on a whole people, down to a word in the market. Then the army marched, and the loss that followed is remembered as the Chhota Ghallughara. Now set beside that a word the Sikh scripture puts in its very first line, describing God: nirvair. Without hate, without enmity. And a line of Guru Arjan in the Granth, here in paraphrase: no one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger; I get along with everyone. That line sits in the same scripture the minister tried to silence. Then look at how the story is kept. The Ardas, the prayer said at the end of gurdwara gatherings, remembers those who gave their lives for the faith. But it remembers them. It doesn't curse anyone. The names of the dead are carried; the hatred isn't. That's the hard lesson tucked inside this terrible year. Grief is not the danger. Grief is what love does when someone is taken. The danger is the moment grief decides someone must pay, and keeps widening the circle of who that someone is. Lakhpat Rai's story shows that moment. The Sikh way of remembering him shows another one: grief without hate.
screen: `GRIEF THAT TURNED TO REVENGE.` · `EVEN A WORD WAS BANNED.` · `NIRVAIR: WITHOUT HATE.` · `REMEMBERED, NOT CURSED.` · then, large: `GRIEF WITHOUT HATE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold grief without hate. Settle, and let your shoulders drop. Bring to mind a loss of your own, or a wrong done to someone you love. Not the worst one. One you can hold for two minutes. Let the sadness be there. Then notice whether there's a second thing riding along with it: a wish that someone would pay. Don't fight it. Just see it, and gently set it a little apart from the grief, the way you'd set down a heavy bag beside you. Keep the love. Loosen the grip on the blame. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.

nirvair, without hate. Tradition says a minister's grief for his brother became a vow of revenge against a whole people, even though the opening line of Sikh scripture names God this way. Today's word.
Your line: grief without hate. Today, if something stings, name the hurt out loud to yourself, and refuse to widen the circle of who's to blame. Day eight hundred fifty-seven.

858.title: The protection system
858.hook: the Khalsa offered villages protection in return for a share of the harvest
858.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of the Khalsa's duty to protect the weak, and Sikh groups today organize practical help for neighbors in need, regardless of faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a minister's grief for his brother became a war on a whole people, and the Sikh memory of it carries the dead without a curse. Your line was grief without hate. Did a hurt try to turn into blame? Day eight hundred fifty-eight.

Harvest time in a Punjab village, in the hard years. The wheat is in. And everyone in the village knows what can happen next. Raiders from outside. A local strongman's men. Tax collectors who take far more than the tax. There's no police to call, and the government in Lahore is either far away or part of the problem. Then a group of Sikh horsemen rides in, and their leader makes an offer to the village elders. Pay us a share of the harvest, and no one touches this village. If anyone does, they answer to us. Today's word is the name of that offer: rakhi.
screen: `HARVEST IN.` → `NO ONE TO CALL.` → `AN OFFER AT THE GATE.`

segments.voice: Rakhi is a Punjabi word for guarding, keeping watch, protection. And in these years it became the name of a system. Tradition describes it like this. A Sikh band would take a village under its rakhi. The village paid a share of its crops at harvest. In return the band promised to keep the village safe from plunder, by anyone. Notice what that means for a community that, only a few years earlier, had been living on horseback in forests with a price on its head. The hunted were becoming the protectors. Tradition says villagers who had never taken amrit, Hindu and Muslim as well as Sikh, now looked to the Khalsa to keep their harvest safe. It isn't a simple story. Some readers see in rakhi an early shape of the Sikh states that would come later: protection, then loyalty, then land. Some point out that a band that collects a share for safety is holding real power over the village, and that power can be used well or badly. Sikh tradition remembers the ideal and measures the bands against it. Where does that ideal come from? The Sikh scripture keeps describing God as the one who protects, the keeper, the shelter of those who have no shelter. And Sikh teaching holds that the Khalsa is there to defend the weak. A line of Guru Arjan in the Granth, in paraphrase, says the Lord has become the protector, and no one can harm the one he keeps. Rakhi took that and made it an everyday job: walking a village's boundary, answering when someone called for help. Sikhs today don't collect a harvest share. But the job survives in a smaller shape: knowing your neighbors, and being someone they could come to. Keep the village safe.
screen: `RAKHI: GUARDING, PROTECTION.` · `A SHARE OF THE HARVEST FOR SAFETY.` · `THE HUNTED BECAME PROTECTORS.` · `POWER, USED WELL OR BADLY.` · then, large: `KEEP THE VILLAGE SAFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: protect one neighbor. Sit comfortably, and breathe. In your mind, walk the boundary of your own small village: your street, your building, your floor, your team. Who lives along it? Let faces come. Now notice one who might need a little looking after. Someone older, someone alone, someone new, someone having a hard month. Don't plan a rescue. Just pick one person, and one small way to keep watch: a knock, a message, a carried bag. If you pray, you can hold them in your mind and say Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Rakhi. Protection. The system in which Sikh bands guarded villages from plunder in return for a share of the harvest. Today's word.
Your line: keep the village safe. Today, do one small thing that makes your neighbor's day safer or easier, without being asked. Day eight hundred fifty-eight.

859.title: The Dal Khalsa, 1748
859.hook: at a Sarbat Khalsa in Amritsar the bands united into one army under Jassa Singh Ahluwalia
859.howItsDone: Sikhs still speak of the Sarbat Khalsa, a gathering of the whole community at Amritsar, as the place where the Panth decides together in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rakhi: Sikh bands guarding villages from plunder for a share of the harvest. Your line was keep the village safe. Who did you look out for? Today, the bands themselves face a choice. Day eight hundred fifty-nine.

Horsemen are riding into Amritsar from every direction. Each group has its own leader, its own banner, its own story of the hard years. Some leaders have never ridden together. Some have quarreled. Each band has kept itself alive by being quick and independent, answering to no one but its own chief. Now they are all dismounting at the same place, near the Harmandir, for a gathering Sikhs call the Sarbat Khalsa: the whole Khalsa, together. On the table is a question that asks a lot of proud people. Should each of us keep riding alone? Today's word is the answer they gave: Dal Khalsa.
screen: `BANDS RIDE IN FROM EVERY SIDE.` → `EACH WITH ITS OWN CHIEF.` → `SARBAT KHALSA: THE WHOLE KHALSA.`

segments.voice: Dal means an army, a host. Dal Khalsa: the army of the Khalsa. This path met the name once before, alongside the gurmata, the decision the gathering makes together. Today, look at what the decision cost. Tradition says it was Nawab Kapur Singh, the humble leader who had once been fanning the sangat, who pressed for it. The scattered bands would become one army. They wouldn't disappear. Each chief kept his own band, his own riders. But they would answer to one command, and gather again at Amritsar to decide things together. And as the head of that one army, the gathering chose Jassa Singh Ahluwalia. So every chief in that gathering gave something up. Not his men, not his name, but the right to do whatever he liked. That's the hard part of unity. It's easy to agree that we'd be stronger together. It's much harder to be the one who steps back so it can happen. Where did the Sikhs get the nerve to try? From something older than the army. Guru Gobind Singh had founded the Khalsa as one body, with one initiation, drinking from one bowl. And the Sikh scripture speaks again and again of the sangat, the company of the faithful, as the place where the Guru is found. The Dal Khalsa took that spiritual idea and gave it saddles. There's something else worth noticing. The gathering decided in front of the Harmandir, with the Granth present. Sikhs understand those decisions as made in the Guru's presence, not just as a vote of the strongest. When the bands rode out of Amritsar, they rode out as one army.
screen: `DAL: AN ARMY, A HOST.` · `EACH CHIEF STEPPED BACK A LITTLE.` · `UNITY IS EASY TO PRAISE, HARD TO DO.` · `DECIDED IN THE GURU'S PRESENCE.` · then, large: `ONE ARMY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: join with others. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a group you belong to: a family, a team, a congregation, a group chat that's gone quiet. Notice where you've been riding alone in it, doing things your own way and waiting for the others to catch up. Ask honestly: what would I have to give up, a little, for this group to move together? An opinion held too tight, a habit, the need to be in charge. Don't decide anything yet. Just let yourself see it, and breathe with it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, and hold the group in mind. The bell holds the time.
Dal Khalsa. The army of the Khalsa: tradition says the scattered Sikh bands joined it at a Sarbat Khalsa in Amritsar, under Jassa Singh Ahluwalia. Today's word.
Your line: one army. Today, in one group you're part of, step back a little so the whole can move together. Day eight hundred fifty-nine.

860.title: Jassa Singh Ahluwalia
860.hook: a leader honored as the king of the community
860.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Jassa Singh Ahluwalia as Sultan-ul-Qaum, and his story is told in gurdwara talks and Sikh history lessons as an example of a leader formed by kirtan and seva.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the scattered bands became the Dal Khalsa, and every chief stepped back a little. Your line was one army. Where did you let the group move together? Today, the man they chose to lead it. Day eight hundred sixty.

A boy is singing in a household in Delhi. His father has died, and his mother has brought him a long way from Punjab, to the home of Mata Sundari, Guru Gobind Singh's widow, the woman whose letters guided the scattered sangats. Tradition says she took the boy in, and that the household got used to hearing him sing the morning hymns. Years later, that boy would ride at the head of the Dal Khalsa, and Sikhs would give him a title that sounds like a crown. Today: Jassa Singh Ahluwalia.
screen: `A FATHERLESS BOY IN DELHI.` → `MATA SUNDARI TAKES HIM IN.` → `HE SINGS THE MORNING HYMNS.`

segments.voice: The title was Sultan-ul-Qaum. Sultan is a king, and qaum is a people, a community, a nation. The king of the community. It's a big name. So it's worth looking at how tradition says he grew into it, because none of it starts with a crown. It starts with a song. In Mata Sundari's house, tradition says, he learned kirtan, singing the Guru's hymns, and he kept singing them all his life. Then he was handed on to Nawab Kapur Singh, who led the Sikh bands. Under him, tradition says, the boy worked: looking after horses, serving in the langar, the free kitchen, doing the jobs nobody writes poems about. Kapur Singh watched him, and in time named him as the one to carry the leadership on. So by the time the gathering at Amritsar chose him to head the Dal Khalsa, he had been formed by two people who led by serving: a widow who kept the community together with letters, and a nawab who fanned the congregation. And that's the shape of leadership Sikhs prize in him. The Sikh scripture is wary of rulers who think power makes them great. Guru Nanak, in a hard line here in paraphrase, compares the kings of his day to tigers and their officials to dogs. Jassa Singh's story is told as the other kind. Notice too that the title is about the qaum, the people, not the land. A sultan of a country owns ground. A leader of the qaum carries people. Sikhs remember him, among other things, as a fighter who stood at the front, and as a man who was, tradition says, still singing the morning hymns. A leader of the qaum.
screen: `SULTAN-UL-QAUM: KING OF THE COMMUNITY.` · `RAISED BY MATA SUNDARI, SINGING KIRTAN.` · `SERVING UNDER NAWAB KAPUR SINGH.` · `A LEADER WHO CARRIES PEOPLE.` · then, large: `LEADER OF THE QAUM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: lead by serving. Settle, and breathe slowly. Think of somewhere you have a little say, even a small one: a family dinner, a project, a friend group, a shift at work. Picture the people there. Now ask: what's the job nobody wants, the horse nobody grooms, the dish nobody washes? Let one come to mind. See yourself doing it, quietly, before anyone asks. Notice how that changes the way you'd speak to the group afterward. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Jassa Singh. Raised, tradition says, in Mata Sundari's household and trained by Nawab Kapur Singh, he led the Dal Khalsa and was honored as Sultan-ul-Qaum, king of the community. Today's word.
Your line: leader of the qaum. Today, wherever you have any say at all, do the unglamorous job first, then speak. Day eight hundred sixty.

861.title: Abdali's invasions
861.hook: Ahmad Shah Abdali came down through Punjab again and again
861.howItsDone: Sikhs close the Ardas, said at the end of gurdwara gatherings and in daily prayer, by asking for chardi kala, rising spirits, through the Name, and tell the stories of the eighteenth-century Khalsa as stories of chardi kala.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a boy raised on kirtan grew into Sultan-ul-Qaum. Your line was leader of the qaum. Did you do the plain job first? Today the week ends, with a storm that kept coming back. Day eight hundred sixty-one.

Dust on the road from the northwest. A farmer in Punjab straightens up in his field and watches it. He has seen this before. A huge army is coming down out of Afghanistan, across the rivers, heading for the riches of Delhi. It will pass through his land on the way there and on the way back. And then, some time later, the dust will rise again. The king at the head of that army was Ahmad Shah Abdali, and Punjab lay across his road. Today: Abdali's invasions.
screen: `DUST FROM THE NORTHWEST.` → `AN ARMY BOUND FOR DELHI.` → `AND THEN IT COMES AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Ahmad Shah Abdali was the king of Afghanistan, and he invaded northern India again and again. Each time, his army marched through Punjab. For the people who lived there, that meant crops taken, towns emptied, captives carried off. And then the army would go home, and the land would try to recover, and then it would come back. So the question for the Sikhs wasn't how to win one battle. It was how to keep going through a storm that returns. Tradition and history describe the answer they found. The Dal Khalsa mostly didn't stand in the road and meet the full army head on. They let it pass, and struck its edges and its rear, especially on the way home, when it was heavy with plunder and captives, the same tactic this week's story of Nadir Shah's captives showed. And when the army left, they came back out of the forests and took the countryside again. Each return of the storm was met with another return of the Khalsa. Sikhs have a phrase for the spirit that makes that possible, one this path met in the forests, and it comes in the Ardas, the prayer said at the close of gurdwara gatherings: chardi kala. Rising spirits, a spirit that keeps climbing. The Ardas asks that through the Name there be chardi kala. It isn't cheerfulness. It's the refusal to stay knocked down. Look back at this week through that lens. A father and son who would not give up their faith. Captives brought home. Grief held without hate. Villages kept safe. Scattered bands made into one army, and a leader who carried his people. Each one was a way of standing up again. Abdali came again and again. So did they.
screen: `A KING WHO KEPT COMING BACK.` · `STRIKE THE EDGES, THEN RETURN.` · `CHARDI KALA: RISING SPIRITS.` · `A WEEK OF STANDING UP AGAIN.` · then, large: `AGAIN AND AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: breathe through a repeated challenge. Sit comfortably, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind something that keeps coming back in your life. A worry that returns every Sunday night. An argument that circles round again. A habit that slips back in. Notice how tired you are of it. That's allowed. Now, on each breath in, say to yourself: again. And on each breath out: and again. Not as a complaint. As a way of standing up one more time. If you pray, you can say Waheguru instead. The bell holds the time.
Abdali's invasions. The Afghan king's armies came through Punjab again and again, and the Khalsa met each return by returning too, in the spirit the Ardas calls chardi kala. Today's word.
Your line: again and again. Today, when the same hard thing shows up one more time, meet it one more time, with one breath before you do. Day eight hundred sixty-one.
